SK1006 Use a using declaration

A using block that runs to the end of its enclosing block is a using declaration.

CategoryModernization
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSyntax
Needs a compilationno
Runs under --load=looseyes
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, safe
Language version floorC# 8.0
Since1.2
ReSharperConvertToUsingDeclaration (resharper_convert_to_using_declaration_highlighting)
SupersedesIDE0063

Why

A using statement whose block is the rest of the scope is a level of indentation that buys nothing: the object is disposed at the closing brace either way. Written as a declaration it loses the nesting, and in a method that acquires three things it loses three levels of it. The rule fires only where the two closing braces are the same program point, because a using declaration disposes when its enclosing block ends and moving that point later is a behaviour change rather than a style one.

Example

Instead of:

void Write(string path) {
    using (var stream = File.OpenWrite(path)) {
        stream.WriteByte(0);
    }
}

Write:

void Write(string path) {
    using var stream = File.OpenWrite(path);
    stream.WriteByte(0);
}

When it does not fire

None known. It is silent unless the using statement is the last statement of its enclosing block — anywhere else the object would be disposed later than it is now — and silent when the rewrite would lift a declaration into a scope where the name is already taken. That second guard scans the whole member rather than only what is in scope, because foreach (var item in xs) { } standing beside using (…) { var item = 2; } is legal today and CS0136 once the braces are gone, and a lookup at the statement cannot see it. It is also silent on using (existingVariable), which has no declaration to convert, on a body that is not a block, and wherever the statement contains a preprocessor directive, since the fix deletes two braces.
